title: What One Hotel Review Tells You About a Hundred Missed Calls
summary: Reachability complaints show up in about 3 of every 1,000 hotel reviews. The written complaint is the exception, not the measure. Why the review count hides the problem.
body_markdown:
The problem is not what appears in the reviews. It is what never appears. The review count is not the size of the problem, it is the visible edge of a much larger one.


The review is a weak instrument here by construction, not by accident. Reachability shows up in about 0.3% of reviews, and most hotels never receive enough reviews for an event that rare to register. Non-group independents make up about 72% of the DACH market, and a typical one collects a median of around 21 reviews across a 90-day window. A problem that appears in three of every thousand reviews cannot surface at a property that gathers twenty of them in a quarter. The arithmetic guarantees that the complaint stays invisible at exactly the hotels that make up most of the market.


The behaviour compounds the arithmetic. A guest who cannot reach a hotel rarely writes about it, because by the time a review is an option, the guest has already solved the problem another way.[The call that goes unanswered](https://www.codyco.ai/blog/the-state-of-hotel-missed-calls) does not sit and wait. It becomes[a booking at the hotel next door](https://www.codyco.ai/research/hotel-phone-report-2026) , a conversation with an OTA agent, an email that lands hours after it mattered, or an arrival the front desk was never warned about. None of those outcomes produces a review that says the hotel could not be reached. Most of them produce no record at all.


This is what the silence costs. The same gap shows up as softer occupancy on quiet nights, as a heavier reliance on OTAs than the hotel would choose, and as no-shows and late cancellations with no reason attached. Each of those is read as market conditions or ordinary guest behaviour, and the phone is never the first suspect. The hotel's numbers move while the review page stays quiet.


The sharpest proof runs through the hotels that removed the human on purpose. Self-service and no-desk hotels carry reachability complaints at roughly double the rate of staffed and independent hotels, about 5.4% of hotels against 2 to 3%. When there is no front desk, being reachable by phone is not a nicety on top of the service, it is the fallback the whole model depends on, so the failure surfaces where it usually stays hidden. The genuine complaints at these properties describe the moment the automation failed and there was no person to reach: a guest locked out, a key box or check-in machine that would not work, an emergency number that rang out, a channel that only ever replied by app. The severity runs higher too. These are the reviews where a guest gives one star and books somewhere else next time.


The complaint that does get written is not a measure of how often the problem happens. It is what is left after almost everyone affected has moved on without a word. Reading the review count as the size of the problem is like counting the guests who complained about a cold room and calling that the number of cold rooms.
